The corpus search surfaces one paper that is squarely about "genus surfaces topology," plus two others that touch the phrase more incidentally. I have enough from the paragraph excerpts to answer directly and precisely.

## Answer

The phrase "genus surfaces topology" points overwhelmingly to a single paper in the corpus, with two adjacent papers using the same vocabulary in different mathematical contexts.

### Primary source — dynamical systems on genus-*p* surfaces

**`0706.2397.pdf` — "Inversely Unstable Solutions of Two-Dimensional Systems on Genus-*p* Surfaces and the Topology of Knotted Attractors"** (title, p. 1).

This paper studies the topology of attractors for 2-dimensional dynamical systems living on closed orientable surfaces of arbitrary genus *p* (a *p*-hole torus). Its concrete results:

- **Setup and goal.** It generalizes an earlier result (Martins, 2004) from the torus to higher-genus surfaces: instead of a single invariant set, several attractors can coexist and even be linked on a higher-genus surface, and the paper studies the topology of these attractors (p. 2). On a torus with one unstable cycle, an attractor *A* is not homeomorphic to a circle if there is an inversely unstable periodic orbit; "it is in this form that we shall generalize the result to higher genus surfaces" (p. 3).

- **Constructing the systems.** The most general C^∞ systems on a genus-*p* surface are built from a fundamental domain in the upper-half-plane (hyperbolic) model, using automorphic functions invariant under linear fractional transforms; inversely unstable periodic motions become **knots** on the genus-*p* surface (p. 4).

- **Topological constraint from index theory.** By the Poincaré index theorem, any dynamical system on a surface of genus *p* > 1 must have at least one equilibrium point, chosen at the cusp points of the fundamental domain (p. 6).

- **Cutting / surgery construction.** Cutting a genus-2 surface (2-hole torus) along a knotted trajectory turns it topologically into a torus with 2 boundary circles (p. 10). Any system on a *p*-genus 2-manifold can be represented on a sphere by cutting each handle along an equilibrium-free fundamental circuit; conversely, higher-genus systems are obtained by performing surgery on spherical ones — gluing in a dissipative region, cutting the attractor, twisting, and re-identifying the ends to make a knot (p. 14).

- **Main counting theorem.** By induction: on the torus the attractor is a band, on a 2-hole torus there are at most 3 attractors, and adding one to the genus introduces one more handle giving at most two more attractors — so a genus-*p* surface has at most **(2*p* − 1)** invariant sets (Lemma, p. 11). Restated: a dissipative system on a genus-*p* surface can have at most *p* topologically distinct knotted attractors, and whether each is homeomorphic to a circle depends on the presence of an inversely unstable solution within it (p. 14).

- **Conclusion.** The study covers dynamical systems on a genus-*p* surface, proves the ≤ (2*p* − 1) bound for a surface with one unstable cycle, and shows that for genus > 1 an individual attractor is not homeomorphic to a circle when it contains an inversely unstable solution; a future extension targets genus-*p* solid 3-manifolds (p. 19).

### Secondary sources (same terms, different topic)

- **`0706.0028.pdf` — "Py–Calabi quasi-morphisms and quasi-states on orientable surfaces of higher genus"** (p. 1). This is symplectic topology, not dynamical-systems topology: it works on a closed oriented surface *M* of genus *g* ≥ 2 with a symplectic form, defining quasi-morphisms via Morse functions and their Reeb graphs Γ_F (pp. 6, 9, 10, 12, 22), with continuity taken in the C²-topology on C^∞(M) (pp. 32–33). It matches on "genus," "surface," and "topology" but the "topology" here is a function-space topology, not surface topology.

- **`0709.2857.pdf` — (complex/algebraic surfaces, Chern numbers)** (pp. 2–4). Here "surfaces" means *complex* surfaces: it proves that diffeomorphic compact complex surfaces have equal Chern numbers, using the topological Euler characteristic, the Todd genus, and Smale's h-cobordism theorem (pp. 2, 3, 4). "Genus" appears as the *Todd genus* — an invariant — not as the genus of a topological surface.

### Bottom line

If you mean the topology of surfaces indexed by genus, the complete answer is `0706.2397.pdf`: it develops the topology of knotted attractors of 2D dynamical systems on genus-*p* surfaces, with the central result that such a surface supports at most (2*p* − 1) invariant sets / at most *p* distinct knotted attractors, tied together by index theory and cut-and-surgery constructions (pp. 1–19). The other two papers reuse the words "genus," "surface," and "topology" but in symplectic (`0706.0028`) and complex-algebraic (`0709.2857`) settings.
